summary: Liberia lies in West Africa, founded in 1847 by freed African Americans from the United States, the first republic in Africa, and has experienced two civil wars.

ranking.name: Christianity
ranking.description: From 1822 the American Colonization Society moved freed American Black people to Liberia, bringing Protestant faiths such as the Baptist, Methodist and Anglican churches, and after the founding of the state in 1847 Christianity became the religion of the ruling elite. American missionary groups set up schools and hospitals in the interior, so Christianity spread along with education; in the late 20th century and during the civil war (1989–2003), Pentecostal and independent churches expanded rapidly.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Islam was introduced several hundred years ago by Mandingo (Malinke) traders from what is now Guinea and Mali, and is found mainly in the north and west, with believers mainly Mandingo and Vai. During the civil war, disputes over land and citizenship between the Mandingo and other ethnic groups led to religious and ethnic tensions.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: Liberian society is strongly religious, churches and mosques are the center of community life, and those who explicitly say they have no religion are very few, mainly a small number of young people in cities.

ranking.name: Traditional beliefs
ranking.description: Many Liberians, while believing in Christianity or Islam, still take part in traditional secret societies and ancestral spirit rites, so those who follow only traditional religion are few in the statistics, but the influence of traditional beliefs is far greater than this figure.

religion.background: Liberia's indigenous ethnic groups each have their own traditional beliefs and secret societies (such as the men's Poro society and the women's Sande society), which are responsible for initiation rites and social education. Islam was introduced several hundred years ago from the West African interior to the north and west by Mandingo traders. From 1822 the American Colonization Society moved freed Black people and free Black people from the United States here, bringing Protestant faith; the Republic of Liberia was founded in 1847, and the elite of Americo-Liberians took Christianity as a mark of "civilization" and spread it through mission schools. Today Christianity accounts for the vast majority of the population, but traditional beliefs and customs and the secret societies still deeply influence social life.

ranking.name: English (including Liberian English)
ranking.description: English came with the freed Black American settlers after 1822, and after the founding of the state it was the sole official language and the language of schools and government. Native English speakers are mainly descendants of the Americo-Liberians, but Liberian English (Kolokwa) is widely used as the lingua franca of the various ethnic groups, so the number who can actually communicate in English is far greater than the number of native speakers.

ranking.name: Mandingo
ranking.description: Mandingo belongs to the Mande family, and the Mandingo were originally a trading people active in the West African interior who, several hundred years ago, entered northern and western Liberia through long-distance trade and brought Islam. Mandingo is their mother tongue and is also used by other ethnic groups in market trade.

language.history: Liberia has about 16 major ethnic groups, using languages of the Niger-Congo family such as the Kru, Mande and Mel languages. From 1822 the Americo-Liberian settlers brought American English, and after the founding of the state in 1847 English became the sole official language and the language of education. In the course of contact between the colonization society's settlers and the indigenous people, "Liberian English" (Kolokwa) formed, English-based with West African features, and became the lingua franca among the various groups. In the 19th century the Vai man Duwalu Bukele also invented the Vai script, one of the few scripts indigenously invented in West Africa.

ranking.name: Jollof rice
ranking.description: Rice stewed together with tomato, onion, chili and spices into a red spiced rice, often served with chicken or fish. It is spicy and fragrant, and the rice grains absorb the rich flavor of tomato and spices.
ranking.history: Jollof rice is generally thought to originate in the Wolof Empire (Jolof) of the Senegambia region around the 14th century, from which its name comes. Tomatoes reached West Africa from the Americas only after the 16th century, so the present red version took shape relatively late. It spread throughout West Africa with trade and the movement of people, and Nigeria and Ghana even argue endlessly over whose jollof tastes best; in Liberia it is the star of feasts at festivals such as weddings, Christmas and Independence Day (26 July).

ranking.name: Fufu
ranking.description: Cassava or plantain is cooked and pounded into an elastic dough, a small piece of which is pinched off by hand and dipped into soup. It is sticky and elastic, mild in flavor by itself, and used mainly to accompany soups.
ranking.history: Fufu is a staple common to West and Central Africa; cassava is native to South America and was introduced to Africa by the Portuguese in the 16th century, spreading quickly because it is drought-tolerant and high-yielding, replacing yam in part as the main ingredient of fufu. In Liberia, fufu is often eaten with palm butter stew or pepper soup, traditionally pounded by women with a large mortar and pestle, and is an important part of family and community life.

ranking.name: Pepper soup
ranking.description: A spicy clear soup of fish, chicken or goat meat cooked with plenty of chili and spices, believed to drive out cold and cure illness. The broth is clear but extremely hot, and often eaten with rice or fufu.
ranking.history: Pepper soup is common in all the coastal countries of West Africa, and the Liberian version uses local chilies and is very spicy. People often drink pepper soup to restore their health when they have a cold or after childbirth, and it is also a snack to accompany drinks at gatherings. This soup reflects the history of how West African chili, introduced by the Portuguese from the Americas in the 16th century, was quickly integrated into the local diet.

ranking.name: Palm butter stew
ranking.description: Meat or fish is stewed in a thick "palm butter" cooked down from palm fruit pulp and served with rice, with a rich flavor. The sauce is orange-red, with the distinctive aroma of the palm fruit.
ranking.history: The oil palm is native to West Africa and has been an important local source of fat for thousands of years. During the European Industrial Revolution of the 19th century, palm oil became an important export commodity of Liberia and West Africa, used to make soap and machine lubricants. In the home, women boil and pound palm fruit to extract a thick sauce for stews, so palm butter has become one of the most representative home dishes of Liberia.

ranking.name: Cassava leaf stew
ranking.description: Cassava leaves are pounded or chopped and stewed with palm oil, chili and meat or fish into a thick dark green stew, served with rice. It is rich and spicy, and is one of Liberia's most common home dishes.
ranking.history: After the Portuguese introduced cassava to West Africa in the 16th century, local people ate not only the tuberous root but discovered that the leaves are rich in protein and vitamins, and so developed cassava leaf stew. In Liberia and Sierra Leone, cassava leaf is a very common Sunday family dish. During the civil war of the 1990s, large numbers of Liberian refugees settled in places such as Minnesota and Rhode Island in the United States, also bringing this dish to communities abroad.
